pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11. The classic two-hip classification of dinosaurs — Saurischia ('lizard-hipped') vs Ornithischia ('bird-hipped') — taught by SORTING skeletons on a single pelvic character and then confronting the famous irony (birds came from the lizard-hipped group).
• Standards — UK (DfE): Y6 Evolution & inheritance and the KS2 working-scientifically strand of 'grouping and classifying'; connects to KS3 classification.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-LS4-2 (anatomical similarities/differences used to infer relationships) and the nature-of-science practice of constructing/critiquing classifications from evidence.
• Operational details: focus on the pubis — in Saurischia it points forward/down (incl. theropods AND sauropods); in Ornithischia it points backward, parallel to the ischium (Stegosaurus, Triceratops, Iguanodon, hadrosaurs). Stress the naming trap: the BIRD-hipped group did NOT give rise to birds — birds evolved from the LIZARD-hipped theropods (backward pubis in birds arose convergently). Introduce that the scheme itself was challenged (2017 Ornithoscelida) — classifications are hypotheses that can change.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (concrete, ~9): sort several dinosaurs into two piles using the hip picture. Tier B (transitional, ~10): explain which way the pubis points for each group. Tier C (formal, ~11): explain why 'bird-hipped' misleads — birds descend from lizard-hipped theropods — and note the classification has been debated.
bestPractices: Teach classification as sorting by a diagnostic CHARACTER (the pubis direction), not by memorising which animal is which.
Surface the naming irony deliberately — it is a memorable hook and corrects the natural but wrong assumption.
Use familiar exemplars in each bin (theropods+sauropods vs Stegosaurus/Triceratops/hadrosaurs) so the groups feel concrete.
Introduce the 2017 Ornithoscelida reshuffle to model that classifications are revisable hypotheses, not fixed facts.
Keep to the single pelvic character at this age; avoid overloading with the full suite of skeletal synapomorphies.
keyRepresentations: Paired pelvis diagrams: pubis forward/down (Saurischia) vs pubis backward (Ornithischia).
A two-bin sorter populated with well-known dinosaurs.
A simple family-tree twig showing birds nested inside lizard-hipped theropods.
A 'name vs reality' callout: 'bird-hipped' ≠ 'ancestor of birds'.
A before/after tree graphic illustrating the Ornithoscelida rearrangement.
commonMisconceptions: 'Birds came from the bird-hipped dinosaurs' — they came from lizard-hipped theropods; the backward pubis in birds is convergent.
'Meat-eaters are one hip group and plant-eaters the other' — sauropods (plant-eaters) are lizard-hipped alongside theropods.
'The hip name describes diet or size' — it describes pelvis anatomy only.
'Dinosaur classification is fixed and settled' — the traditional split has been actively challenged (Ornithoscelida).
'All bird-hipped dinosaurs are closely related to birds' — they are the group MORE distant from birds.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11: teach the classic two-group dinosaur classification — Saurischia ('lizard-hipped') vs Ornithischia ('bird-hipped') — by sorting skeletons on a single diagnostic character, the direction the pubis bone points. Learners classify by evidence rather than memorising names, then confront the naming irony (birds descend from the LIZARD-hipped theropods, not the bird-hipped group) and meet the idea that the scheme itself was challenged in 2017, so a classification is a revisable hypothesis.

activities.title: Palaeontologist's hip-sorting table
feedback: For the dinosaurs in this set, a pubis that points forward/down marks Saurischia (lizard-hipped), and a pubis shaft that swings backward parallel to the ischium marks Ornithischia (bird-hipped). This is a guide rule rather than a law: some later lizard-hipped theropods (such as Velociraptor, and birds) also evolved a backward pubis.

If a learner separates T. rex and a sauropod into different bins because they look so different, show that both share the lizard-hipped pubis — appearance does not define the group, hip structure does.

A pigeon's pubis really does point backward, so sorting by the hip character alone reasonably lands it in 'bird-hipped' — this is exactly where the simple character rule diverges from the evolutionary story. Reveal that birds are nonetheless lizard-hipped theropods by ancestry: their backward-pointing pubis arose separately (convergently) from the one in Ornithischia, which is why the hip shape alone misleads here and the 'bird-hipped' name does not mark the bird ancestors.
Point out the pattern once the bins fill: fierce meat-eating theropods and giant plant-eating sauropods are BOTH lizard-hipped, so the groups are not meat-eaters vs plant-eaters.
activities.rationale: Classification is an act of sorting by a diagnostic character and getting feedback. Letting the child decide each case, then revealing the pattern, makes the defining character salient and turns the naming irony into a discovered surprise rather than a stated fact. The pigeon case also shows, at an age-appropriate level, that a single character can diverge from evolutionary relationship because of convergent evolution; the activity should make clear the phylogenetic answer comes from ancestry, not from the hip-shape rule itself. An interactive sorter that highlights the pubis and recomputes the piles as each animal is placed makes the mechanism concrete; rotating or zooming each pelvis (optional) helps read the bone, though the character reads adequately in a clear side view.
sourceClaims: Dinosaurs are traditionally divided into Saurischia (lizard-hipped, pubis pointing forward; includes theropods and sauropods) and Ornithischia (bird-hipped, pubis pointing backward; includes Stegosaurus, Triceratops, ornithopods).
Despite the name, birds evolved from the lizard-hipped theropods, not from the bird-hipped ornithischians; the backward-pointing pubis in birds arose convergently.
learnerActions: Examine each dinosaur's pelvis and trace which way the main shaft of the pubis bone points: forward-and-down, or swung backward alongside the ischium. (Some bird-hipped dinosaurs, such as Triceratops and duck-bills, also have a forward-pointing prepubic blade, so look for the backward shaft lying beside the ischium.)
Place each dinosaur into one of two bins: 'lizard-hipped' (Saurischia) or 'bird-hipped' (Ornithischia).
Sort a set that includes theropods (e.g. T. rex) AND sauropods (long-necks like Brachiosaurus) — both lizard-hipped — alongside Stegosaurus, Triceratops and duck-billed hadrosaurs — all bird-hipped.
As a final specimen, examine and classify a modern pigeon's pelvis, then check where it actually belongs in the evolutionary tree.
State in your own words the rule you used to decide each group.
activities.intendedInsight: In the classic two-group scheme, these dinosaurs can be sorted using one diagnostic anatomical character, the orientation of the pubis bone, not diet, size or overall appearance. Scientists also use many other characters. The group names describe hip shape, and the 'bird-hipped' label does NOT mean that group gave rise to birds. In fact birds are lizard-hipped theropods whose backward pubis evolved independently.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal: two hips side by side
feedback: Forward/down pubis = Saurischia (lizard-hipped), e.g. theropods and sauropods.

Backward pubis shaft parallel to the ischium = Ornithischia (bird-hipped), e.g. Stegosaurus, Triceratops, hadrosaurs. In Triceratops and hadrosaurs a forward prepubic blade is also present, and the backward shaft is short.
activities.rationale: A clean, labelled paired diagram teaches the diagnostic character directly and is a useful scaffold or reference. It is best paired with the sorting activity, because a fixed pair of examples lets the learner read the character but does not itself require classifying multiple new specimens.
sourceClaims: Dinosaurs are traditionally divided into Saurischia (lizard-hipped, pubis pointing forward; includes theropods and sauropods) and Ornithischia (bird-hipped, pubis pointing backward; includes Stegosaurus, Triceratops, ornithopods).
learnerActions: Look at two labelled pelvis diagrams placed side by side: one with the pubis pointing forward/down, one with the pubis swung backward.
Tap each pubis to see its direction emphasised, then reveal the group name and example animals for that hip type.
Before revealing, predict the group name from the pubis direction alone.
activities.intendedInsight: In the classic scheme, the key feature taught for telling the two groups apart is the direction of the pubis bone. For typical members, each direction maps to a group name and a familiar set of examples, although some later lizard-hipped theropods (and birds) evolved a backward pubis.

activities.title: Why the family tree was re-argued
feedback: If a learner treats dinosaur grouping as settled, point to the 2017 Ornithoscelida proposal as an example of the traditional split being actively challenged.
A good explanation notes that classifications are inferences from anatomical evidence and can be revised when that evidence is reinterpreted.
activities.rationale: Introducing the Ornithoscelida reshuffle models the nature-of-science idea that classifications are revisable. A narrated or dialogue form can add historical colour and reasoning; it complements, rather than replaces, the hands-on sorting that builds the core classifying skill.
sourceClaims: A 2017 study (Baron, Norman & Barrett) proposed the Ornithoscelida hypothesis, reorganising the traditional Saurischia/Ornithischia split — showing the classification is an actively debated hypothesis.
learnerActions: Read or listen to a short account of why the two-group scheme was proposed and why a 2017 study (the Ornithoscelida hypothesis, Baron, Norman & Barrett) proposed reorganising it.
Compare a simple before/after family-tree sketch showing the traditional split and the proposed rearrangement.
Explain in one or two sentences why even a long-established classification can change when new evidence is weighed.
activities.intendedInsight: A classification is a hypothesis built from evidence, not a fixed fact; scientists actively debate and revise how dinosaurs are grouped.

activities.title: Check: naming trap and the sorting rule
feedback: Birds evolved from the LIZARD-hipped theropods (Saurischia), not the bird-hipped group. This surprises people because a bird's own pubis points backward (bird-shaped), yet that backward pubis evolved separately (convergently) — so by ancestry a bird is a lizard-hipped theropod. The group names describe the hip anatomy of the dinosaur groups, and 'bird-hipped' does not mark the bird ancestors.
The deciding feature is the pubis direction; diet and size do not determine the group, which is why carnivorous theropods and herbivorous sauropods are both lizard-hipped.
T. rex and Brachiosaurus share the forward/down pubis, so both are Saurischia despite looking very different.
activities.rationale: A two-tier check (classify, then explain) discriminates a learner fooled by the names from one who grasps the diagnostic character. Recognition items confirm the sort; the explanation prompts elicit the reasoning that reveals the naming irony is understood. Recognition alone does not elicit the learner's own explanation, so the explain prompts are needed.
sourceClaims: Despite the name, birds evolved from the lizard-hipped theropods, not from the bird-hipped ornithischians; the backward-pointing pubis in birds arose convergently.
learnerActions: Answer: which group did birds evolve from — lizard-hipped or bird-hipped — and why is that surprising?
Sort several named species into Saurischia and Ornithischia.
Answer: what single feature do you look at to decide a dinosaur's group?
Explain: T. rex (a fierce meat-eater) and Brachiosaurus (a gentle long-neck) are in the SAME hip group — how can that be?
activities.intendedInsight: Secure understanding is shown by correctly classifying by hip structure AND explaining that the group names describe pelvis anatomy, not bird ancestry or diet.

constraints: Keep to the single pelvic character (pubis direction) at this age; do not overload learners with the full suite of skeletal synapomorphies.
Teach classification as sorting by a diagnostic character, not as memorising which animal belongs where.
The tap-to-reveal paired diagram is a scaffold/reference: it lets learners read the character but does not require classifying new specimens, so pair it with active sorting.
Recognition-only or multiple-choice checks confirm the sort but do not elicit the learner's own explanation of the naming irony; include a short explain-in-your-own-words prompt for the formal level.

When using the pigeon case, make clear that a bird's pubis genuinely points backward and that the lizard-hipped classification comes from ancestry plus convergent evolution — do not imply the pigeon is 'wrongly' placed by the character or that the learner erred by using the taught rule.

Keep the pigeon/convergence nuance consistent across activities: wherever the naming trap is answered, note that a bird's own pubis points backward yet it descends from lizard-hipped theropods, so learners do not treat hip-shape grouping and evolutionary grouping as identical.
Present the 2017 Ornithoscelida proposal as an example that classifications are debated/revisable, not as a settled replacement for the two-group scheme.

Address the specific misconceptions directly: birds came from the bird-hipped group; groups are meat-eaters vs plant-eaters; the hip name describes diet or size; dinosaur classification is fixed; all bird-hipped dinosaurs are close relatives of birds (under the traditional scheme they are the group more distant from birds; the 2017 Ornithoscelida proposal would instead place them closer to theropods and birds than sauropods are).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all three cited sources carry verified:false in the row and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source claims were migrated as exact copies and attached only where they directly support the stated teaching principle; they do not establish comparative efficacy of any one activity format.

The row's legacy framing asserted that 'dialogue cannot deliver' hands-on classifying and that 3D 'adds nothing essential'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to scoped affordances (sorting builds the active classifying skill; narration adds reasoning; 3D/zoom aids bone-reading).
'Convergent evolution' of the backward pubis in birds is a substantive claim presented at an age-appropriate level ('arose separately'); it is sourced to AMNH but unverified here.

The pigeon 'click moment' depends on the diagnostic pubis character diverging from phylogeny for birds: a strict character sort places a bird in 'bird-hipped' because its pubis points backward, while the evolutionary answer (lizard-hipped theropod) rests on ancestry. Feedback across activity[0] and the check was aligned so this is presented as convergence rather than as the learner being fooled by the name.

Iguanodon, named individually in the source as an ornithopod exemplar, is covered under 'hadrosaurs/duck-bills (ornithopods)' rather than named; this is a minor exemplar simplification, not a content change.

probeDeeper: T. rex is a fierce meat-eater and Brachiosaurus is a gentle giant — yet they're in the SAME hip group. How can that be?
Why doesn't the name 'bird-hipped' tell you which dinosaurs became birds?
What single feature do you look at to decide which group a dinosaur belongs to?
assess.correctAnswer: Birds evolved from the LIZARD-hipped group (Saurischia — specifically theropods like T. rex), NOT the bird-hipped group, even though 'bird-hipped' sounds like it should be the bird ancestors. The two groups are defined by hip-bone structure, not by which became birds.

errorPatterns.pattern: Birds came from the bird-hipped dinosaurs — 'the name says so.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Expose the naming trap: the label describes hip shape; birds actually descend from lizard-hipped theropods.
errorPatterns.distractor: Birds came from the bird-hipped group, because they're called bird-hipped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses Ornithischia because the word contains 'bird.'

errorPatterns.pattern: Dinosaurs are grouped by what they ate or by size, not by hips.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redirect to the defining criterion — hip-bone arrangement — and show carnivores and herbivores fall in both groups.
errorPatterns.distractor: The two groups are the meat-eaters and the plant-eaters.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the two groups are meat-eaters and plant-eaters, or big and small.

errorPatterns.pattern: T. rex and a long-necked sauropod must be in different groups because they look so different.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that hip structure, not overall appearance, defines the group — both share the lizard-hipped arrangement.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses to place theropods and sauropods together in Saurischia.

responseLevels.gap: Groups dinosaurs by diet or size, or has no basis, and cannot name the two groups.
responseLevels.full: Classifies species correctly by hip structure AND explains the naming irony — birds arose from lizard-hipped theropods, so the labels describe hip shape, not bird ancestry.
responseLevels.partial: Names Saurischia and Ornithischia and knows it's about hips, but misassigns species or is fooled by the 'bird-hipped' label into thinking those became birds.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Dinosaurs are split into two groups by their hip bones: 'lizard-hipped' (Saurischia) and 'bird-hipped' (Ornithischia). Which group do you think birds evolved from — and why might that answer be surprising?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child misled by the names picks 'bird-hipped.' A child who understands the classification knows it was lizard-hipped theropods, and can explain the labels describe hip shape, not ancestry.
